title: Cross-SKU interference & latency profile: A100 / H100 / L40S (multi-cloud, driver matrix)
content:
Summary:

This is a working note documenting cross-SKU latency and interference behavior we observed when running the inference runtime across A100, H100 and L40S cloud SKUs with multiple driver/CUDA combinations. The primary goal was to find characteristic failure modes and tail-latency amplifiers that are not visible in single-SKU isolated benchmarks. High-level takeaways:

- H100 gives higher peak token throughput for long-context workloads but is more sensitive to driver/firmware and PCI topology, producing larger p99 variability under bursty arrivals.
- A100 is the most consistent across driver versions and shows smaller tail amplification under CPU/GPU contention, but lower peak throughput for 32k+ contexts.
- L40S (cloud inference-optimized cards) has low power draw and predictable latency for short-context interactive workloads but exhibits throughput cliffs when NVMe swap or host PCIe bandwidth saturates.
- Driver 535.x (where available) reduced observed tail-latency on H100 by ~10–15% relative to older 520.x stacks in our experiments, likely due to improved nvlink aggregation and kernel scheduling.

Motivation / why this feels missing:
- Our prior SKU sweeps focused on steady-state throughput (tokens/s) and 50/95th latencies. We lacked a focused multi-sku interference matrix that stressed host-side contention (CPU, NIC, NVMe) and compared driver versions in combination with firmware. Customers report intermittent p99 spikes in production that do not reproduce in isolated benches — this doc is an attempt to bridge that gap.

Test matrix (short):
- Models: Llama2-13B-chat (float16), together with a smaller Llama2-7B for control.
- Context lengths: 512, 4k, 16k, and 32k.
- Batch sizes: 1 (interactive), 4, 16, 64 (throughput modes).
- SKUs/cloud: AWS p4d.24xlarge (A100 40GB NVLink), AWS p5.24xlarge (H100 SXM), GCP a2-highgpu (A100 PCIe), GCP l4 (L40S).
- Drivers/CUDA: CUDA 11.8 + driver 520.x, CUDA 12.1 + driver 535.x (where supported), a pinned baseline with NVIDIA drivers provided by cloud image (varies by cloud).
- Interference modes: (a) colocated CPU synthetic load (sysbench CPU 90% on host cores), (b) NIC saturation (iperf UDP bursts up to 50% bw), (c) NVMe stress (fio random-read/write), (d) background container preemption (Docker restart churn)
- Replicates: 5 runs per cell, collect p50/p95/p99 token latencies, GPU util %, SM occupancy, PCIe read/write MB/s, host CPU steal/steal time, power draw (where supported).

Method notes (short):
- Runtime: Redwood inference container with continuous-batching disabled for interactive runs, enabled for throughput. We used identical model artifacts and quantization settings.
- Measurement hooks: runtime tracing for per-token emit times, nvidia-smi polled at 250ms, perf (NVIDIA NSYS) traces for selected runs (heavy).
- Environment controls: pinned CPU affinities for worker processes when testing the non-interference baseline; NUMA binding enabled for NVLink topologies on AWS.

Key observations (detailed):
1) Tail latency amplification under CPU contention
- When host CPU cores are loaded (~>80% sysbench), A100 setups increased p99 by ~18% for batch=1, 4k context; H100 setups increased p99 by ~30%. L40S had a ~12% increase.
- Root cause trace-level evidence: increased scheduling latency in the host process (longer syscall latencies) which delays the next token emission and causes the runtime to accumulate small stalls inside the token loop. H100 + older driver stacks showed syscall wakeup jitter correlated with GPU kernel launch queuing.

2) NVMe / PCIe cliff with long-context checkpoints
- For 16k and 32k contexts on L40S (GCP L4 with PCIe-attached GPU), we observed sudden throughput drops when host read/write IO increased (fio 70% random-write load). The runtime pins large KV cache pages to host memory and relies on PCIe bandwidth; under saturation the per-token latency increased >3x and throughput fell ~55%.
- A100 NVLink setups (p4d) are much more resilient; NVLink effectively hides host PCIe bursts for KV operations.

3) Driver/firmware idiosyncrasies on H100
- On H100 SXM instances we saw greater variance across driver versions. Driver 535.x reduced p99 by ~12% in our runs for large batches and long contexts. NSYS traces show improved small-kernel queuing behavior and fewer micro-waits. There remains a firmware + driver interaction that causes power/clock clamping under short bursts — visible as short drops in SM clocks that increase latency.

4) Inter-node network bursts (traffic) and model-waterfall effects
- When serving multi-token streaming with many concurrent requests, saturating the NIC created small pauses in the serving process (UDP/packet loss increased syscalls); this effect is most pronounced when combined with high pinned CPU load. The interplay is worst on PCIe-A100 hosts with busy host network stacks.

Representative numbers (selected):
- Llama2-13B, context=4k, batch=1 (interactive):
  - AWS p4d (A100 NVLink) driver 520: p50=78ms, p95=140ms, p99=225ms
  - AWS p5  (H100 SXM) driver 520: p50=62ms, p95=170ms, p99=360ms
  - AWS p5  (H100 SXM) driver 535: p50=60ms, p95=150ms, p99=300ms
  - GCP l4 (L40S PCIe) driver 520: p50=90ms, p95=160ms, p99=280ms
- Throughput (tokens/s) long-context heavy (32k, batch=16): H100 ~1.65x A100 on same model under best driver, but p99 tails were ~1.4x worse without driver 535.

Engineering implications and quick wins:
- Default to drivers with latest CUDA (12.1 / 535) for H100 fleets; schedule a controlled rollout and monitor p99 during ramp. Our data shows measurable tail improvements.
- For interactive short-context workloads, prefer L40S-class instances for cost predictability, but pin host IO and avoid colocating heavy NVMe work on the same host.
- Enable NVLink topologies (where available) for large-context models — NVLink materially reduces host PCIe sensitivity for KV/cache traffic.
- Add a runtime guardrail: detect host IO pressure (simple host counters) and dynamically reduce KV prefetch window or fall back to smaller batch packing to reduce PCIe demand.

Open questions / next experiments:
- Re-run matrix with RDMA-enabled NICs (AWS EFA/GCP EFA) to see if NIC offload reduces syscall wakeup jitter under network bursts.
- Test with different kernel CPU governors and isolated CPU islands (cset) to prevent host scheduler from interfering with token-stepping.
- Repeat H100 driver rollout test on another cloud region/zone to rule out firmware variations between physical host inventories.
- Explore whether MIG partitioning (when feasible) reduces tail-amplification in multi-tenant Dedicated pools.

Action items / proposed roadmap (short):
- (Priya) prepare a constrained driver rollout playbook for eng-run (week of 11/04).
- (Marco) add host IO pressure signal to runtime telemetry and a small experiment toggling KV window (ETA 2 weeks).
- (Evelyn) schedule NSYS traces for H100 535 vs 520 across three physical hosts to triangulate firmware impact (ETA 10 days).
- (Jasper) run RDMA-enabled NIC experiments with p99 focus (blocked on infra ticket).

Notes to reviewers:
- This is a working document — some numbers are medians from limited runs and will be expanded. Focus review on the hypotheses and recommended guardrails rather than the absolute numbers (we will publish a reproducible matrix once we lock infra).

Appendix (short):
- Scripts used: /infra/benchmarks/sku-interference/ (internal repo, see linked PR).
- Quick references: SERV-2912 (customer p99 report), PR-842 (runtime tracing hooks), confluence page for full run artifacts.

Unresolved curiosities / heuristics observed (informal):
- H100 seems to hide queuing inside short kernel bursts; the runtime's naive batching increases the probability of hitting those micro-waits. Slightly randomizing batch composition reduced observed p99 in some runs (worth experimenting systematically).
- Host NIC driver behavior matters — sometimes identical NIC bandwidth produced different p99 profiles across images (cloud image/kernel variation).

End of note.
